claims.text: Annealing a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy at 200–600 °C causes its metastable solid solutions to partially decompose.
The decomposition produces stable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes and reorganizes the matrix composition.
Precipitation-induced compositional changes alter the composition and stability of protective oxide and passivation layers.
The altered surface films become more adherent or protective under corrosive and oxidative conditions.
Annealing reduces the corrosion rate in chloride media relative to the non-annealed baseline.
Annealed alloys have lower corrosion current densities than otherwise comparable as-cast or non-annealed alloys.
Annealing enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the non-annealed baseline.
Annealed alloys exhibit slower mass gain or oxide-scale growth at temperatures of at least 200 °C.
The initial as-cast or rapidly consolidated alloy contains a retained metastable solid solution together with minor intermetallic phases.
The target alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
A sufficient Mg content promotes formation of stable precipitated phases during annealing.
The proposed mechanism depends on the presence of non-equilibrium phases before annealing.
Departures from the specified Mg content, initial non-equilibrium state, or density constraint may alter phase decomposition and passivation behavior.
Exact phase fractions, precipitation kinetics, and interfacial compositional changes remain insufficiently quantified across different thermal histories.
